channel.title: Felix blog
channel.description: Notes from building Felix: how it works, why it is built the way it is, and what testing it has turned up.

item.title: Fast, without losing messages
item.description: How Felix answers a fsynced publish in a third of a millisecond, writes at the disk's full rate under load, and slows publishers down instead of dropping their messages.

item.title: Before you loosen the timeout, run the old commit
item.description: Intermittent failures in Felix's cluster tests kept turning out to be real bugs in the broker, so before loosening a timeout I now run the test against a commit from before the suspect change; three cases show what that finds.

item.title: Acknowledged, then forgotten: a crash under periodic fsync
item.description: Under Felix's default periodic fsync, a crashed broker could come back missing records it had acknowledged while the cluster still counted it as caught up; this is how review and the TLA+ model found it on the follower and leader sides, and what the fix costs.

item.title: How we catch a 1% regression
item.description: Felix's rule is that a release must not be measurably slower than the one before it; this is how same-runner A/B runs, a Welch's t-test and throwaway bisect PRs in GitHub Actions find a 1-2% loss, and why a single benchmark run can't.

item.title: Our model said everything passed. It was checking nothing.
item.description: Felix checks 107 TLA+ configurations in CI; this is about three times a passing check meant nothing, and the twin configurations, reachability checks and spec pairing we use to catch it.

item.title: One slow subscriber shouldn't slow anyone else
item.description: How Felix keeps one slow subscriber from holding up publishers or other readers, and how a 2% single-publisher loss came from where the feeder gave back a subscriber's byte budget.

item.title: The data came back
item.description: Deleting a Felix stream or cache and creating one with the same name could bring back the old one's data; this is how incarnations fixed it, and how we kept control-plane members on different releases from storing different answers during the rollout.

item.title: Point your Kafka client at Felix
item.description: Felix brokers speak enough of the Kafka wire protocol for Kafka producers and partition-assigning consumers to use durable Felix streams; this is how a Kafka request becomes a Felix operation, how idempotent sequences survive a failover, and exactly where compatibility stops.

item.title: Ten parcels, one envelope: Linux UDP GSO and Felix's MTU cap
item.description: Raising Felix's QUIC MTU on Linux stalled delivery for good, because UDP GSO turns ten packets into one datagram the kernel refuses and quinn never falls back; this is how we found it, why the cap is 6,550, and why 4,096 is the default.

item.title: Introducing Felix: one log for streams, caches and counters
item.description: What Felix is, how a publish travels from a client to disk to every subscriber, why it is built that way, and how to run it on your laptop in five minutes.
